questions.question: Spatial resolution in radiography refers to:
options: The color saturation of the image
The ability of the system to distinguish two nearby anatomical details
The total light intensity of the image after development
The actual physical dimension of the imaged object
questions.explanation: High resolution allows better precision and fineness of anatomical details.

questions.question: The optical density of a radiograph mainly depends on:
options: The amount of radiation absorbed by the receptor
The rotation speed of the anode at startup
The sharpness of image contours
The physical size of the sensor used
questions.explanation: It represents the degree of blackening of the image after exposure and processing.

questions.question: Increasing the kilovoltage (kV) results in:
options: An increase in overall contrast
A drastic reduction in the emitted dose
A longer required exposure time
A decrease in contrast
questions.explanation: A high kV increases photon energy, promoting beam penetration, which decreases contrast (grayer image).

questions.question: What role does milliamperage (mA) play during acquisition?
options: It controls the beam intensity and the number of photons (dose)
It determines the quality of tissue penetration
It adjusts the focal-object distance
It manages the speed of digital data storage
questions.explanation: mA regulates the number of electrons striking the anode, thus the beam intensity and overall darkening.

questions.question: Why strictly limit exposure time?
options: To increase the optical density of the image
To reduce the risk of kinetic blur related to patient movement
To artificially improve spatial resolution
To reduce the kV power required
questions.explanation: The longer the time, the higher the probability of patient movement, degrading image sharpness.

questions.question: The standard focal-film distance is chosen to:
options: Avoid Compton scattering phenomena
Increase the parasitic anode effect
Reduce geometric magnification and improve accuracy
Decrease the total dose received by the patient
questions.explanation: A longer distance allows a more faithful projection of the anatomy by limiting magnification.

questions.question: The anode effect (Heel effect) corresponds to:
options: A loss of sharpness on the edges of the image
A parasitic reflection of the beam on the film
An absorption by the lead collimator
A variation in beam intensity between the anode and cathode side
questions.explanation: Radiation intensity is lower on the anode side than on the cathode side due to self-absorption by the target.

questions.question: The Heel effect is particularly pronounced when:
options: The focal-film distance is short
The kilovoltage is very low
The milliamperage is high
The exposure time is very long
questions.explanation: It is accentuated by reduced distances or small anode angles.

questions.question: What is an extraoral radiograph?
options: An examination performed without any ionizing radiation
An image where the sensor is positioned outside the oral cavity
A technique reserved exclusively for endodontics
A microscopic analysis of soft tissues
questions.explanation: Panoramic or teleradiography are typical examples of extraoral imaging.

questions.question: The principle of stereoscopic radiography relies on:
options: The use of two offset images to create a perception of depth
The digital fusion of two images taken at different energies
The systematic use of intravenous contrast
A classical linear tomography technique
questions.explanation: The offset allows obtaining a perception of depth (3D vision) by exploiting parallax.

questions.question: The postero-anterior (PA) view is useful for:
options: Screening for proximal caries
Analyzing dynamic dental occlusion
Studying facial symmetry and frontal sinuses
Visualizing the TMJ in thin slices
questions.explanation: It provides an overview of the facial mass and a right/left comparison.

questions.question: The Blondeau view is primarily dedicated to the exploration of:
options: Maxillary sinuses
Mandibular condyles
Parotid glands
Mandibular canals
questions.explanation: It clears the maxillary sinuses by projecting the petrous ridges below the sinus floor.

questions.question: The Hirtz view offers a:
options: Strict profile view of the facial mass
Oblique view of the ascending rami
Frontal view of the orbits
Axial (basal) view of the skull base
questions.explanation: It allows study of the skull base, zygomatic arches, and sphenoid sinuses.

questions.question: The Schüller view is classic for visualizing:
options: The temporomandibular joint (TMJ)
The apices of maxillary molars
The maxillary sinus as a whole
The nasal fossae
questions.explanation: It is historically used for radiological assessment of the TMJ.

questions.question: TMJ arthrography consists of:
options: Performing a simple profile view without any artifice
Injecting a radiopaque contrast agent into the joint space
Using a high-resolution CT without injection
Performing a dynamic functional ultrasound
questions.explanation: This allows visualization of the shape, position, and perforations of the articular disc.

questions.question: Sialography allows visualization of:
options: The overall morphology of temporary teeth
The drainage of frontal sinuses
The arterial vascularization of the skull
The ductal network of salivary glands
questions.explanation: A radiopaque agent is injected into the excretory duct to opacify the ductal system.

questions.question: Fistulography is indicated for:
options: Exploring the course of a fistula by injecting contrast agent
Measuring the length of dental roots
Screening for asymptomatic deep cavities
Checking osseointegration of an implant
questions.explanation: It allows locating the deep origin of a fistulized infectious process.

questions.question: Cephalometry is a standardized technique used for:
options: The diagnosis of occlusal caries
The detailed study of pulpal structure
The analysis of craniofacial relationships
The measurement of periodontal tooth mobility
questions.explanation: Essential for orthodontics and orthognathic surgery planning.

questions.question: Cephalometric tracing consists of:
options: Artistic detailed drawing of the profile
Measurement of angles and distances between precise anatomical points
A 3D volumetric radiograph
A rapid CT examination
questions.explanation: It allows objective quantification of skeletal and dental discrepancies.

questions.question: The Sella point (S) is located at the center of:
options: The sella turcica
The root of the nose
The anterior nasal spine
The mandibular angle
questions.explanation: It is a fundamental cranial reference point in cephalometry.

questions.question: The Nasion point (N) corresponds to:
options: The upper edge of the orbit
The bottom of the chin
The frontonasal suture
The tip of the nasal spine
questions.explanation: The most anterior point of the frontonasal suture on the midline.

questions.question: Point A (subspinale) designates:
options: The deepest point of the maxilla on the midline
The summit of the mandibular symphysis
The posterior nasal spine
The middle of the incisor crown
questions.explanation: It is the reference point for the sagittal position of the maxilla.

questions.question: Point B (supramentale) designates:
options: The bony point of the chin
The angle of the jaw
The deepest point of the mandibular concavity
The upper alveolar border
questions.explanation: It is the reference point for the sagittal position of the mandible.

questions.question: The Gonion point (Go) is located at the level of:
options: The head of the condyle
The angle of the mandible
The middle of the chin
The apex of the lower incisor
questions.explanation: It defines the junction between the lower border and the posterior border of the mandible.

questions.question: The Frankfort plane connects:
options: The sella turcica and the nasion
The gonion and the menton
Point A and point B
The porion and the orbitale
questions.explanation: It is a theoretical horizontal reference used for cranial orientation during tracing.
